content: Riboflavin, also known as vitamin B2, is a water-soluble micronutrient that plays a critical role in maintaining the health of animals, including humans. It is a central component of the cofactors flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and flavin mononucleotide (FMN), which are essential for the function of all flavoproteins. These cofactors are involved in a wide range of cellular processes, including energy metabolism and the metabolism of fats, carbohydrates, and proteins. Riboflavin is found in foods such as milk, cheese, leafy green vegetables, liver, legumes (e.g., mature soybeans), yeast, and almonds. However, it is sensitive to light exposure, which can degrade its potency. Riboflavin is not toxic when consumed orally, as its low solubility limits absorption to safe levels. Even at high dietary doses, excess riboflavin is excreted in the urine, often giving the urine a bright yellow color. Toxic doses can only be achieved through injection, but this is not relevant to typical nutritional intake. Industrially, riboflavin is synthesized using various microorganisms, including filamentous fungi like Ashbya gossypii, Candida famata, and Candida flaveri, as well as bacteria such as Corynebacterium ammoniagenes and Bacillus subtilis. Genetically modified strains of Bacillus subtilis have been developed to enhance riboflavin production and include antibiotic resistance markers. These strains are used commercially to produce riboflavin for food and feed fortification. For example, the chemical company BASF operates a plant in South Korea specializing in riboflavin production using Ashbya gossypii. In these modified strains, riboflavin accumulates to such high concentrations that it forms crystals in the vacuoles, which can eventually rupture the fungal mycelium. Riboflavin is yellow or orange-yellow in color and is used both as a food coloring agent and as a fortifying ingredient in various food products. It is commonly added to baby foods, breakfast cereals, pastas, sauces, processed cheese, fruit drinks, vitamin-enriched milk products, and some energy drinks. Riboflavin is also widely included in multivitamin supplements, often in quantities exceeding the daily requirement. The excess is excreted in the urine, causing a bright yellow coloration within hours of ingestion. Due to its poor water solubility, riboflavin is challenging to incorporate into liquid products, necessitating the use of riboflavin-5'-phosphate, a more soluble but more expensive form. Riboflavin deficiency, or ariboflavinosis, occurs when dietary intake is insufficient. This deficiency is relatively common because riboflavin is continuously excreted in the urine. However, it is usually accompanied by deficiencies in other vitamins. Riboflavin deficiency can be primary, due to inadequate dietary sources, or secondary, resulting from conditions that impair intestinal absorption, hinder the body's ability to utilize the vitamin, or increase its excretion. Symptoms of riboflavin deficiency in humans include cracked and red lips, inflammation of the mouth and tongue, mouth ulcers, cracks at the corners of the mouth (angular cheilitis), and a sore throat. Other symptoms may include dry and scaling skin, fluid accumulation in mucous membranes, and iron-deficiency anemia. The eyes may become bloodshot, itchy, watery, and sensitive to bright light. Riboflavin deficiency is classically associated with the oral-ocular-genital syndrome, characterized by angular cheilitis, photophobia, and scrotal dermatitis. In animals, riboflavin deficiency leads to stunted growth, failure to thrive, and eventual death. Experimental riboflavin deficiency in dogs results in growth failure, weakness, ataxia, and inability to stand, followed by collapse, coma, and death. Dermatitis and hair loss develop during the deficiency state, along with corneal opacity, cataracts, hemorrhagic adrenal glands, fatty degeneration of the kidneys and liver, and inflammation of the gastrointestinal mucosa. Post-mortem studies in rhesus monkeys fed a riboflavin-deficient diet revealed significantly reduced riboflavin levels in the liver, the primary storage organ for this vitamin in mammals. Overt clinical signs of riboflavin deficiency are rare in developed countries, but subclinical deficiency may occur, particularly in children, the elderly, individuals with eating disorders, and those with certain medical conditions such as HIV, inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes, and chronic heart disease. Subclinical deficiency in children can impair growth, and it has also been observed in women taking oral contraceptives. Riboflavin levels in the body can be assessed by measuring erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity, which serves as a diagnostic test for riboflavin deficiency. Clinically, riboflavin has been used in various therapeutic contexts. For over 30 years, riboflavin supplementation has been part of phototherapy treatment for neonatal jaundice. However, the light used in this treatment also degrades riboflavin in the infant's blood. More recently, riboflavin supplementation has shown promise as an adjunct to beta-blockers in the treatment of migraine headaches. Additionally, riboflavin is being explored for its potential to improve the safety of transfused blood by inactivating pathogens. Riboflavin binds to nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) in cells, and when exposed to light, it breaks these nucleic acids, effectively killing the cells. This technology has been demonstrated to inactivate a broad spectrum of pathogens, including viruses, bacteria, and parasites, in all major blood components (platelets, red blood cells, and plasma). Riboflavin is also used in corneal collagen crosslinking (C3R) to treat keratoconus, a progressive corneal disorder. In this procedure, riboflavin drops are applied to the corneal surface, and ultraviolet A (UVA) light is used to induce collagen crosslinking, which strengthens the cornea. Studies have shown that this treatment can stabilize keratoconus progression.
